newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan victors hang more ex-officials, chase foes.
newsitem.headline: Afghan victors hang more ex-officials, chase foes.

text.p: Afghanistan's new self-declared Taleban Islamic government said on Saturday it had hanged two more ex-officials and that its forces were pursuing ousted President Burhanuddin Rabbani north of the capital Kabul.
Official Kabul Radio said two "accomplices" of former Afghan president Najibullah were hanged on Friday evening, naming them as Najibullah's bodyguard, General Jafsar, and his aide Tokhi.
Najibullah and his brother Shahpur Ahmadzai were themselves executed soon after the Taleban entered Kabul on Friday.
All four had been housed at a United Nations compound in Kabul since Najibullah was ousted in April 1992.
The fly-blown bodies of Najibullah and Shahpur were still hanging on Saturday from a concrete traffic post outside the presidential palace. But there was no sign of the bodies of Jafsar and Tokhi.

Afghanistan's ousted government on Friday called on the world not to recognise the fundamentalist Islamic regime decreed by the Taleban militia, which moved quickly to bar women workers from offices and promised death for adulterers and drinkers.
However, the United States expressed hope that the Taleban would move toward national reconciliation and held out the possibility of establishing full diplomatic ties.
Kabul Radio also urged those who had fled the capital fearing bloodshed to return.
A Taleban preacher at a mosque in the diplomatic Wazir Akbar Khan district said all men should wear either the traditional skull caps or turbans to conform with strict Islamic tenets.
Religious scholar Mullah Agha Gulabi told the radio that adulterers and drinkers must be killed.
"God says that those committing adultery should be stoned to death," he said.

"Anybody who drinks and says that it is not against the Koran, you have to kill him and hang his body for three days until people say this is the body of the drinker who did not obey the Koran and Allah's order."
Heavily-armed Taleban fighters patrolled Kabul in pick-up trucks on Saturday, but there was no sign of tension as Kabul resumed normal life after the Friday weekend.
Kabul Radio said government employees should report for work as usual. But one employee who turned up at the Ministry of Reconstruction with his colleagues found the doors locked.
A military helicopter circled over the city early in the morning, apparently heading for Kabul airport, which has been unused for the past year.
International relief agencies said they hoped to begin flights from Kabul airport as soon as they received security clearances from the Taleban.

Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai, the ousted government's deputy foreign minister, told the United Nations that ousted President Rabbani and his advisers had retreated north to Parwan and Kapisa provinces and were contemplating their next move.

Reading a statement issued by Rabbani, Ghafoorzai said that "the Islamic State of Afghanistan declares that any administration to be announced by this group, dependent on the outside, will have no legal or Islamic law credibility and therefore, will be rejected by the Afghan nation".
Ghafoorzai, attending the U.N. General Assembly session in New York, blamed neighbouring Pakistan for the Taleban's success.
Pakistan's U.N. ambassador, Ahmad Kamal, said the old Afghan government was finished and the Taleban was in control of Kabul.
Pakistan appeared to signal the first recognition of the new regime on Friday by announcing it would dispatch officials for talks in Kabul.
The U.N. Security Council may discuss Afghanistan when it meets on the Middle East crisis on Saturday, but some diplomats believed no action would be taken until Monday.

The Taleban now appear to control well over half of the central Asian country, which has been the scene of continual fighting between various Moslem and ehtnic groups since Soviet troops supporting a communist government withdrew in 1989.

At the U.N. a draft statement prepared by Russia expressed grave concern about the "scale and the intensification of the military confrontation in Afghanistan, including the seizure of the capital city of Kabul by the Taleban."

The statement warned against attempts to impose a military solution in Afghanistan, called for an immediate halt to fighting and urged all Afghan leaders "to renounce the use of force, to put aside their differences and to engage in a political dialogue."
Taleban sources, quoted by an Afghan news service in Pakistan, said militia fighters had chased Rabbani's forces and were fighting at Charikar, capital of Parwan province.

There were no immediate details of the fighting, but the Taleban appeared to be taking aim at the Jabal-us-Seraj base of Rabbani's top military commander Ahmad Shah Masood, which lies to the north of the capital.

The Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted a statement issued by Rabbani from an undisclosed place as appealing to people and faction leaders to resist the Taleban, which earlier appealed for international recognition of its government.
